title: Ushas, the dawn
hook: a night-shift nurse walks out into a sky going pink. The Rig Veda sings to that light, Ushas, the dawn, and it's why Hindus greet the morning sun
carry: sandhya: dawn is holy, shared by every generation
tomorrow: a man swears off the dice. why does he go back?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vasishtha asked Varuna, what did I do? A wrong breaks rita, and honest asking mends it.

The hospital doors slide open and a nurse steps out after a long night shift. Her feet hurt. Her head is full of beeping. Then she looks up. The sky over the parking lot is going from gray to rose to gold, and for a second she forgets everything else. The birds have started. A bus hisses at the corner. Plenty of mornings like this go by unseen. The Rig Veda's poets turned to that light, gave it a name, and sang to it. Today, Ushas, the dawn.
screen: `OUT OF THE NIGHT SHIFT.` → `GRAY, ROSE, GOLD.` → `THE POETS SANG TO IT.`

segments.voice: In the Rig Veda, Ushas is a goddess, pictured as a young woman in bright clothes, driving away the dark. One hymn to her begins, in paraphrase: this light has come, the fairest of lights. Her bright sign is born. Then the poet notices time. The night has made room for the dawn, like a sister giving way to her sister. And then this line. Gone are the mortals who watched the earlier dawns. Now she is seen by us. And coming are those who will see her in mornings still ahead. Three groups of people under one light: those before us, us, and those after. Every sunrise, on this reading, joins them. Later the hymn wakes everyone up. Rise, it says. The breath of life has come back to us. The dark has gone away. Light is coming near. She has opened a path for the sun to travel. And she is ancient and young at once, the hymn says, coming again and again. Here's why that matters in a Hindu home. Dawn is a sandhya, one of the day's holy junctions, with noon and dusk. For many Hindus it's a time to bathe, pray, and pour water toward the rising sun. The poets taught that morning light isn't just weather. It's sacred, and it's shared: whoever greets it stands where their grandparents stood, and where their grandchildren will.
screen: `USHAS: THE DAWN, A GODDESS.` · `THOSE BEFORE, US, THOSE AFTER.` · `ANCIENT AND YOUNG AT ONCE.` · `SANDHYA: A HOLY JUNCTION OF THE DAY.` · then, large: `THE DAWN IS HOLY, AND SHARED.`

segments.voice: Turn toward the east or a window if you can, or call a dawn you remember to mind. Do what many Hindus do each morning: if you have a cup of water, lift it toward the light and pour a little slowly into a plant; if not, just lift your open hands. Hold three people in that light: someone before you who saw this sky, someone with you now, someone who will see it after you. If you pray, greet the morning in your own words.
What the Rig Veda is. Hymns that sing to Ushas, the dawn, fairest of lights, seen by those before us, by us, and by those still to come.
screen: `WHAT THE RIG VEDA IS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Carry this: sandhya. The dawn is holy, and its light is shared by every generation. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Hindu practice, dawn is often a time of prayer: bathing, chanting, and offering water to the rising sun, and the hymns to Ushas are part of the Rig Veda's recited text.

notes: Rig Veda 1.113 paraphrased throughout (no PD translation on the validator list). Confirm verse numbers, especially 1.113.13 (ancient, ever young) and 1.113.16 (rise, the breath of life).
'The fairest of lights' is the hymn's own superlative (1.113.1).
Ushas pictured as a young woman in bright clothes is a standard summary of her hymns, not a quotation. Confirm.
Kutsa as the seer of 1.113 (trapdoor) is from the tradition's index; confirm.
howItsDone mentions offering water to the rising sun (arghya, often with the Gayatri); confirm.
